questions.problem: Given that $8$, $2x$, and $x$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The first three terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=8,\,{a}_{2}=2x,\,{a}_{3}=x.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{2x}{8}=\frac{x}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{x}{2x}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{4} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $-3,\,33,\,-363,\,…$

II. $4,\,52,\,572,\,…$

III. $-2,\,24,\,-312,\,…$
questions.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{33}{(-3)}=-11 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-363)}{33}=-11\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{52}{4}=13 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{572}{52}=11\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{24}{(-2)}=-12 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-312)}{24}=-13\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence I could be a geometric sequence.

questions.problem:
Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $2,\,4,\,10,\,…$

II. $-5,\,10,\,-20,\,…$

III. $1,\,-4,\,-16,\,…$
questions.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{4}{2}=2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{10}{4}=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{10}{(-5)}=-2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-20)}{10}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-4)}{1}=-4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-16)}{(-4)}=4\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence II could be a geometric sequence.

questions.problem:
Consider the following geometric sequence:

$$
-4,\,16,\,-64,\,256,\,…
$$

The fifth term of this sequence is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225716/assets/84c714b0c37c7f28cb83c59e3455755470ff6aa69da145c80ccea19200b1ad8f.png)

Notice that the sequence is geometric, with a common ratio of 

$$
r=\frac{16}{(-4)}=-4.
$$

So, we can get each term by multiplying the previous term by $-4.$ 

Continuing to list terms of the sequence until we get to the $5$th term, we obtain the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225716/assets/400ef822bd63631f65a4190f8367e84878c03a302c3202a112e9de2858ae4249.png)

Therefore, the $5$th term is $-1\,024.$

questions.worked_solution:
The first three terms are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=\frac{x}{4},\,{a}_{2}=x,\,{a}_{3}=64.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{x}{(\frac{x}{4})}=x\cdot \frac{4}{x}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{64}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{64}{x} \\ 4x & =64 \\ x & =\frac{64}{4} \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$
